names.name: Rochester breaded wings
names.said: Order in Rochester and the counter asks which sauce, not how hot. Country Sweet is a sauce, a brand and an answer.

text.what: A chicken wing dredged in seasoned flour before it goes in the oil, fried until the coating sets hard, then glazed rather than tossed loose — most often in Country Sweet, a sweet-and-tangy sauce a Rochester kitchen built in 1977 that is neither barbecue nor cayenne-and-butter. Breading is the whole argument: seventy miles west, Buffalo puts the wing in the fryer bare. Rochester bars also pour plain cayenne sauce, barbecue, teriyaki and garlic parmesan, so a breaded wing is a coating rather than a single flavour.
text.story:
Country Sweet dates itself to 1977, when Tom Lask worked up a sauce in a Rochester home kitchen; the company's own account calls it neither barbecue nor Buffalo. It sells the sauce in mild, hot and BBQ, and sells the wings hand-breaded. That is the firmest dated fact this project could find for the style.

Everything around it is thin. No published history of Rochester's breaded wing turned up in the sources searched here — no founder, no first bar, no year. The city's documented food identity runs elsewhere: the Garbage Plate, trademarked by Nick Tahou Hots and traced to 1918, and the Zweigle's white hot. Wings sit underneath that, carried by menus rather than by writing about menus.

*Tradition holds —* a half-and-half order comes half in the sweet sauce and half in hot, and a 'hot plate' means the wings and the sides under one pour. This project found no published source describing either, so both stay unverified here.

The rivalry gets stated in print even where the history does not. CITY Magazine, naming Jeremiah's Tavern the city's best wings, wrote: "It's easy to find really good wings on damn near every corner in Buffalo. Around here? A little more challenging."
text.how: Dredge the cut wing in seasoned flour — some shops dip in buttermilk or egg first, some go dry — and drop it in the oil. The coating browns into a shell that holds sauce on its surface instead of soaking it in, which is why a sweet glaze works here and slides off a bare Buffalo wing. Fry, then glaze: Country Sweet goes on as a sticky coat rather than a loose toss in a bowl. Blue cheese and celery come alongside, same as west of here. A tavern that fries bare will say so on the board; breaded and naked both sell in this city.
text.today: Country Sweet runs shops in Rochester and Greece and bottles the sauce for grocery shelves. Bar menus carry long sauce lists beside the house breading: Jeremiah's Tavern, read on 16 September 2026, offered sixteen sauces including Garlic Parm, Cajun Dry Rub, Jamaican Jerk and Korean BBQ, with ten traditional wings at $17.99 and twelve boneless at $16.00. *Inference —* the breading, not the sauce, is what makes the plate legible as Rochester's; the sauce list is the same list every American wing counter now prints.

kin.as: Seventy miles west, frying the same cut bare — the style this one is defined against, and the argument that gives it a name.

confusable_with.tell: Bite the skin. A breaded wing has a flour shell that crunches and stays dry under the sauce; a Buffalo wing has bare skin and the sauce is on it, not in a crust.
Garlic parm names a sauce and travels anywhere. Rochester-style names a coating, and the sauce on top can be anything the bar pours.
